lead: A source never emits one pure wavelength. A laser spans a narrow band; an LED spans tens of nanometres. Glass bends each wavelength slightly differently, and in a single-mode fiber the guided mode also sits a little differently in the core at each wavelength. So the wavelengths inside one pulse travel at different group velocities and arrive at different times. That spreading is chromatic dispersion; the spread Δτ is in ps, and the fiber is described by a dispersion coefficient D in ps/(nm·km). It is not a loss, it is a timing error, and on long single-mode links it sets the bit-rate limit. The coefficient has two parts: a material part from the glass and a waveguide part from the profile.
prereq: You need: group velocity and the V number from Unit 1 (see Unit 1, Foundations: Light Propagation in Fibers), and the idea of a pulse spreading in time from 2.5.

blocks.text: A pulse is not one wavelength. Mode theory gives a propagation constant β for the guided mode. The group velocity is v_g = dω/dβ, so the delay after a length L is τ = L/v_g = L dβ/dω. Because β depends on wavelength, every wavelength in the pulse's band gets a slightly different delay, and the pulse arrives stretched in time.
The dispersion coefficient is that delay change per kilometre per nanometre:

blocks.where: D is the dispersion coefficient in ps/(nm·km); L is the fiber length in km; τ is the group delay in ps; λ is the wavelength in nm. D > 0 means longer wavelengths are delayed more and arrive later.
Δτ is the pulse spread in ps; D is in ps/(nm·km); L is in km; Δλ is the full spectral width of the source in nm.

blocks.text: Sign conventions differ between books: some books take D positive when the longer wavelength arrives first; this book takes it positive when the longer wavelength arrives later. Fix one convention and keep it through a whole calculation. Chromatic dispersion has two sources. Material dispersion comes from the glass index and its dependence on wavelength. Waveguide dispersion comes from how tightly the mode is confined to the core, which also changes with wavelength. The two add:

blocks.where: D_m is the material part and D_w the waveguide part, both in ps/(nm·km), each with its own sign.

blocks.text: The refractive index of silica falls as wavelength rises. Both n and dn/dλ enter the group delay, so the spread depends on the curvature of n(λ):

blocks.where: λ is the wavelength in m; c = 3×10⁸ m/s; n is the core refractive index. The result is in s/m²; multiply by 10⁶ to get ps/(nm·km).

blocks.text: For silica, D_m crosses zero near 1300 nm. It is about −100 ps/(nm·km) at 850 nm, so there the longer wavelength arrives first. It is about +20 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm, so there the longer wavelength arrives last. This curve belongs to the glass. Core doping shifts it a little and nothing more, which is why designers attack the other term.
In a single-mode fiber some power travels in the cladding. How much is set by the V number:

blocks.where: a is the core radius; λ is the wavelength in the same unit; n₁ and n₂ are the core and cladding refractive indices.

blocks.text: As λ rises, V falls, the mode spreads further into the cladding, and its effective index drops toward n₂. That wavelength-dependent confinement changes the group delay, which is waveguide dispersion D_w. For a standard step-index profile it is negative across 1300-1600 nm and only a few ps/(nm·km) in size.

D_w is the part a designer controls, through the core radius a and the index step Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁. Because it is negative, it cancels the rising D_m, and the fiber's zero lands near 1310 nm rather than at the material zero near 1300 nm. Fibers built to move that zero all the way to 1550 nm are covered in 2.8.

blocks.text: The slope near 1310 nm is about 0.09 ps/(nm²·km), so D climbs steeply as you move away from the zero. Δλ is the full spectral width of the source, not its modulation rate. If a laser is quoted in frequency, convert:

blocks.where: λ is the operating wavelength in m; c = 3×10⁸ m/s; Δf is the source linewidth in Hz. At 1550 nm, 10 GHz is about 0.08 nm.

blocks.text: A 0.1 nm laser over 100 km with D = 17 gives 170 ps of spread. An LED with 40 nm at the same D gives 68 ns, which limits the link to a few Mbit/s. That is why wide sources pair with short links. In a multimode link, chromatic spread adds to intermodal spread from 2.5; the two are independent, so combine them root-sum-square, Δτ = √(Δτ_ch² + Δτ_mod²). Polarization mode dispersion (2.7) is a separate, random term.

figure.caption: Chromatic dispersion splits into a material part, whose zero is fixed near 1300 nm by the glass, and a waveguide part, which a designer moves by changing the profile; the two add with their signs to put the fiber zero near 1310 nm.

spec.aria: A tree showing chromatic dispersion as material dispersion plus waveguide dispersion, with the material zero near 1300 nm and the waveguide part tunable by profile design.

examples.question: A 100 km single-mode link runs at 1550 nm with D = 17 ps/(nm·km). The laser linewidth is 0.1 nm. (a) Find the pulse spread Δτ. (b) Estimate the bit-rate limit as 1/(4Δτ). (c) Repeat (a) and (b) for a cheaper laser with a 2 nm linewidth.
steps: (a) Δτ = D L Δλ = 17 ps/(nm·km) × 100 km × 0.1 nm = 170 ps.
The twentyfold wider line gives a twentyfold wider pulse, so about twenty times less bit rate.
examples.answer: 170 ps and 1.47 Gbit/s with the 0.1 nm laser; 3.4 ns and 73.5 Mbit/s with the 2 nm laser.

examples.question: A DFB laser at 1550 nm is specified with a 20 GHz linewidth. What is Δλ, and what spread does it cause over 80 km with D = 17 ps/(nm·km)?
examples.check:
lam = 1.55e-6
c = 3e8
df = 20e9
dl = (lam**2 / c) * df
D = 17.0
L = 80.0
dt = D * L * dl * 1e9
print(round(dl * 1e9, 2))
print(round(dt, 1))

traps: Forgetting the source linewidth. A laser is not monochromatic, and with Δλ = 0 the formula wrongly predicts zero spread.
Feeding a linewidth quoted in GHz straight into Δτ = D L Δλ. Convert to nm first; 10 GHz at 1550 nm is only 0.08 nm.
Adding D_m and D_w as magnitudes. They carry opposite signs over 1300-1600 nm, and that cancellation is the whole point.
Mixing units: D is per km, so L must be in km. Using metres inflates the answer a thousand times.
Confusing chromatic dispersion with intermodal dispersion. Chromatic spread exists even in a single-mode fiber, where there is only one mode but many wavelengths.

quiz.q: Define chromatic dispersion and give its unit.
quiz.a: The spreading of one pulse because its wavelengths travel at different group velocities; D is in ps/(nm·km).

quiz.q: Which two parts add to give D?
quiz.a: Material D_m, from the index-wavelength curve of the glass, and waveguide D_w, from how the mode's confinement changes with wavelength.

quiz.q: Why does an LED link suffer more chromatic dispersion than a laser link with the same D and L?
quiz.a: Δτ = D L Δλ, and an LED's spectral width is tens of nm against a fraction of a nm for a DFB laser. The spread scales directly with that width.

quiz.q: An 80 km link at 1550 nm has D = 17 ps/(nm·km) and Δλ = 0.5 nm. Find Δτ and the 1/(4Δτ) bit-rate estimate.
A laser at 1550 nm is specified as 20 GHz linewidth. Convert to nm.
Why is D_w called the tunable part of chromatic dispersion?
quiz.a: D_w depends on core radius a and index step Δ through the V number, and both are fixed by the preform design. D_m is set by the glass composition and barely moves.

quiz.q: A standard single-mode fiber has D = 0 at 1310 nm, yet D_m there is about +1 ps/(nm·km). Explain.
quiz.a: D_w is negative there, about −1 ps/(nm·km), and cancels D_m. The fiber's zero is where D_m = −D_w, not where D_m itself is zero.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern coherent receivers measure and undo chromatic dispersion in digital signal processing, so a 100 Gbit/s channel can cross hundreds of kilometres of ordinary single-mode fiber without optical compensation. Dispersion-engineered fiber still matters for direct-detection and short-reach links, and in the O-band near 1310 nm where D is close to zero. Hollow-core fiber changes the whole picture because light travels mostly in air, not glass. Search next for 'digital dispersion compensation coherent', 'G.652 dispersion slope' and 'zero-dispersion-shifted fiber'.
